title: Modi Lands in New Zealand Tomorrow for the First Time in Forty Years. He Brings a Trade Deal. The Country Brings a Reckoning.
excerpt: The India-NZ FTA eliminates tariffs on 100 per cent of Indian exports and locks in thousands of skilled migrants annually. But 'butter chicken tsunami' remarks and racist graffiti in Auckland are the backdrop nobody can ignore.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Modi's visit marks the first by an Indian PM to New Zealand in 40 years.
  • The new trade deal eliminates tariffs on all Indian exports to New Zealand.
  • Anti-Indian sentiment in New Zealand has surged, complicating the trade agreement.
  • The FTA aims to double bilateral trade to $5 billion in five years.
  • The agreement includes provisions for thousands of skilled Indian migrants annually.

Trade Agreement Details

Modi will arrive in Auckland on Friday for a two-day state visit — the first by an Indian Prime Minister in nearly forty years. The last time an Indian leader set foot in New Zealand was Rajiv Gandhi's visit in 1986, when the country's Indian-born population numbered in the low thousands. Today, Indians are one of New Zealand's fastest-growing ethnic groups, and the relationship between the two countries has never been more consequential — or more fraught.

The Trade Deal

The visit comes weeks after the two countries signed a Free Trade Agreement that was negotiated in record time. Talks launched in March 2025 and concluded nine months later, making it one of the fastest FTAs India has ever closed.

The numbers are striking. All Indian exports — across 8,284 tariff lines — will enter New Zealand duty-free. In the other direction, 57 per cent of New Zealand's exports to India will be tariff-free from day one, with the rest phased in until 95 per cent of Kiwi goods face zero or reduced duties.

"New Zealand businesses are set to boom with our India Trade Deal," Prime Minister Christopher Luxon wrote on X ahead of Modi's arrival. "Fifty-seven per cent of everything we export to India will be tariff-free from day one."

For Indian exporters, the sectors that stand to gain are wide-ranging: pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, textiles, leather, footwear, and processed food will all get improved access to a high-income Pacific economy. On the New Zealand side, wood products, processed timber, wool, sheep meat, kiwifruit, apples, and manuka honey lead the list. India has agreed to open its market to apples and honey under a free trade agreement for the first time.

The two countries aim to double bilateral trade to $5 billion within five years, up from $1.3 billion in merchandise trade and $2.4 billion including services in the last fiscal year.

> ""New Zealand businesses are set to boom with our India Trade Deal," Prime Minister Christopher Luxon wrote on X ahead of Modi's arrival."

The Backdrop Nobody Can Ignore

But the FTA's most politically charged provision has nothing to do with tariffs. The agreement locks in thousands of skilled Indian migrants each year — a provision that has triggered a backlash in a country grappling with anti-Indian sentiment that has grown sharply over the past year.

Shane Jones, a senior minister in New Zealand's ruling coalition, described the migration provisions as a "butter chicken tsunami" — a remark that drew immediate condemnation from the Indian community and reignited a debate about racial attitudes toward South Asians.

![Rajiv Gandhi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/66/Rajiv2.jpg)

The comment was not an isolated incident. Racist graffiti targeting Indians has appeared at multiple sites across Auckland, including outside a school in Papatoetoe. Far-right groups have disrupted Sikh religious processions, performing haka dances as a form of intimidation. A haka competition featured a performance by a former Māori Party president that was directed at an Indian-origin Member of Parliament, sparking a nationwide debate about where cultural expression ends and racism begins.

What the Diaspora Stands to Gain

For the roughly 250,000 Indians living in New Zealand — and the far larger population considering the country as a destination — the FTA contains provisions that go well beyond goods trade.

The agreement includes chapters on services, investment, and skilled mobility, opening pathways for Indian students, professionals, and entrepreneurs. It also covers cooperation in AYUSH (traditional Indian medicine), tourism, forestry, and horticulture.

Indian IT and business services firms, which already account for a significant chunk of the $1.24 billion in bilateral services trade, will benefit from clearer rules and reduced barriers. The agreement also simplifies customs procedures, with a commitment to clear perishable shipments within 24 hours.

The Strategic Picture

Modi's New Zealand stop is the final leg of a three-nation tour that has already produced significant outcomes. In Indonesia, he signed a $630 million BrahMos missile deal — the third country to buy the Indian-Russian supersonic cruise missile. In Australia, he secured a uranium supply agreement that ended a twelve-year stalemate, and AustralianSuper committed another A$500 million to India's infrastructure fund.

The New Zealand visit fits a deliberate pattern. India is methodically deepening its footprint across the Indo-Pacific, signing FTAs, defence agreements, and investment pacts with countries that share its interest in a rules-based maritime order — and its wariness of China's growing influence in the region.

For New Zealand, the calculus is simpler but no less important: it needs markets beyond China, which has been its largest trading partner but has become an increasingly unreliable one. India, with 1.4 billion consumers and GDP growth above six per cent, is the obvious alternative.

What to Watch

Opportunities for the Indian Diaspora
›250,000 Indians in NZ benefit from new FTA provisions.
›Pathways for students, professionals, and entrepreneurs opened.
›Simplified customs for perishable goods within 24 hours.

Modi is expected to address the Indian diaspora in Auckland and meet business and sports leaders alongside his bilateral talks with Luxon. The conversation will inevitably touch on the anti-Indian incidents — Delhi has privately raised concerns about the safety of its citizens in New Zealand, though it has avoided public confrontation.

The real test of the visit will not be the photo opportunities or the trade statistics. It will be whether two democracies can find a way to grow closer economically while honestly confronting the social tensions that economic integration inevitably creates.
